passages.t: The mighty angel and the seven thunders
passages.happening:
Before the seventh trumpet sounds, the book pauses again, as it did in chapter 7. John sees a new figure: “Then I saw another mighty angel coming down from heaven, wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow above his head. His face was like the sun, and his legs were like pillars of fire” (verse 1).

“He held in his hand a small scroll, which lay open. He placed his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land” (verse 2). He cries out with a voice “like the roar of a lion”, and seven thunders answer (verse 3).

John is about to write down what the thunders said. Then he hears a voice from heaven: “Seal up what the seven thunders have said, and do not write it down” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 9 ended with a bleak verdict: after the first two woes, people still did not repent. Before the last trumpet, the book turns from judgment to witness. This chapter and the next are about the message God gives his people to speak.

The angel is described in words close to the risen Christ of chapter 1 (a face like the sun, feet like fire) and the throne of chapter 4 (a rainbow). He carries heaven's authority. Standing with one foot on the sea and one on the land, he claims the whole world for God. A few interpreters take this angel to be Christ himself. Most take him as a great angel, since he is called an angel and swears by God rather than being sworn by. These notes do not choose.

In his hand is ‘a small scroll’. The Greek word, biblaridion, is a smaller form of the word used for the sealed scroll in chapter 5. And it lies open.

Thunder in the Old Testament is the voice of God. Seven thunders speak. John is ready to write them down, and he is told not to. Even in a book called a revelation, not everything is revealed.
passages.ot:
Thunder as God's voice is the psalm's: “The voice of the LORD is over the waters; the God of glory thunders; the LORD is heard over many waters” (Psalm 29:3). In that psalm the voice of the LORD sounds seven times.

Daniel too was told to close up what he saw: “Go on your way, Daniel,” he replied, “for the words are closed up and sealed until the time of the end” (Daniel 12:9). And Moses taught that “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things revealed belong to us and to our children forever” (Deuteronomy 29:29).
passages.hard:
What did the seven thunders say, and why was John told not to write it down?

Revelation does not tell us, and the silence is part of the message. Interpreters offer several explanations. Some think the thunders announced another series of judgments like the seals and trumpets, which God then sets aside: judgments alone have not brought repentance (9:20-21), so the book turns to the witness of the church. Others see a reminder that even an apocalypse, an unveiling, does not unveil everything. Paul too heard things “that man is not permitted to tell” (2 Corinthians 12:4). Others link it with Daniel's sealed book, and suggest the thunders belong to a time not yet come. These notes do not choose.

What can be said with confidence is this. No one should build a scheme on what God chose not to tell. The chapter's weight falls on what John is told to do: take the open scroll, take it in, and speak.
passages.asks: Ask how you live with the things God has not explained. Ask whether you are more curious about what is hidden than faithful with what is open. And ask what it would mean to trust God with the thunders you will never hear.

passages.happening:
The angel standing on the sea and the land lifts his right hand to heaven (verse 5). He swears by God, “who created heaven and everything in it, the earth and everything in it, and the sea and everything in it”. His oath is short: “There will be no more delay!” (verse 6).

“But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound his trumpet, the mystery of God will be fulfilled, just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Raising the hand was the common gesture of an oath. And to swear by the Creator of heaven, earth and sea is to call the whole created world as witness.

What the angel swears is ‘no more delay’. The Greek word is chronos, time. The King James Version put it as ‘time no longer’. In this setting it almost certainly means no more waiting. It answers the martyrs in chapter 6, who were told to rest ‘a little while longer’ (6:11), where the same word appears. The delay God's people feel is not God's indifference. The end is fixed.

That mattered to the first readers. Some in the early church were mocked for waiting: where is the promised coming? Peter answered that God is patient, giving time for people to turn. Jewish writers of the same time wrestled with God's delay after the temple was destroyed in AD 70.

And what will be fulfilled is ‘the mystery of God’. In the New Testament a mystery is not a puzzle. It is a purpose of God once hidden and now made known. Paul uses the word for the gospel, and for the welcome of the nations into God's people. Here the mystery is God's whole plan for the world, about to be completed at the seventh trumpet, ‘just as He proclaimed to His servants the prophets’.
passages.ot:
The oath echoes Daniel's vision, where a man in linen stood above the waters of the river: he “raised his right hand and his left hand toward heaven, and I heard him swear by Him who lives forever” (Daniel 12:7). In Daniel the answer was “It will be for a time, and times, and half a time.” Here the answer is that the waiting is over.

God himself swears this way in the Law: “For I lift up My hand to heaven and declare: As surely as I live forever” (Deuteronomy 32:40).

And the prophets are God's servants who hear his plan: “Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets” (Amos 3:7).
passages.hard:
If the angel said ‘no more delay’, why are Christians still waiting so long afterwards?

The question is a fair one. Readers answer it in different ways. Whether the chapter looks ahead to events in the first century, in the course of the church's history, or at the very end depends on how the book is read as a whole, and the book page sets out the four ways. On every reading it is a commissioning scene, and these notes do not choose.

Peter's answer to the same question stands for all of them: “The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). These notes set no date, and no one should.
passages.asks: Ask where you are waiting on God, and whether you have taken his patience for absence. Ask what it means that the end of the story is fixed by an oath. And ask whether the waiting has made you more patient with others, or less.

passages.t: Sweet in the mouth, bitter in the stomach
passages.happening:
The voice from heaven speaks to John again: “Go, take the small scroll that lies open in the hand of the angel standing on the sea and on the land” (verse 8).

John goes to the angel and asks for it. “Take it and eat it,” he said. “It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be as sweet as honey” (verse 9).

“So I took the small scroll from the angel’s hand and ate it; and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth, but when I had eaten it, my stomach turned bitter” (verse 10).

“And they told me, ‘You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings’” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
To eat the scroll is to take God's message all the way in, so that it becomes part of the one who speaks it.

It is sweet, because it is God's word. It is bitter, because of what it announces: judgment on a world that will not repent, and suffering for those who bear witness. The gospel has the same shape. It is good news, and it centres on a cross.

Then John is sent again. ‘You must prophesy again about many peoples and nations and tongues and kings.’ To prophesy, in the Bible, includes foretelling, but it is mainly forthtelling: declaring God's word to people. John, a prisoner on a small island, is placed in the line of Israel's prophets who spoke to empires. Jeremiah was appointed over nations and kingdoms. Daniel spoke to the kings of Babylon and Persia.

Whether the little scroll is the same scroll the Lamb opened in chapter 5, now handed to the prophet, or a smaller, separate message, is debated. These notes do not choose. Either way it is open now, and its message is for John to speak. Chapter 11 will show what that witness looks like.
passages.ot:
The eaten scroll is Ezekiel's: “‘Son of man,’ He said to me, ‘eat and fill your stomach with this scroll I am giving you.’ So I ate, and it was as sweet as honey in my mouth” (Ezekiel 3:3). Then Ezekiel went out “in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit” (Ezekiel 3:14).

Jeremiah too ate God's words: “Your words were found, and I ate them. Your words became my joy and my heart’s delight” (Jeremiah 15:16).

And Jeremiah's call was to the nations: “See, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant” (Jeremiah 1:10).
passages.asks: Ask when a true word from Scripture has been both sweet and bitter for you. Ask whether you have taken God's word all the way in, or only tasted it. And ask what it would mean for you to speak it, gently and truly, to the people around you.
